The '''generalized gamma distribution''' is a [[Continuous probability distribution|continuous]] [[probability distribution]] with two [[shape parameter]]s (and a [[scale parameter]]). It is a generalization of the [[gamma distribution]] which has one shape parameter (and a scale parameter). Since many distributions commonly used for parametric models in [[survival analysis]] (such as the [[exponential distribution]], the [[Weibull distribution]] and the [[gamma distribution]]) are special cases of the generalized gamma, it is sometimes used to determine which parametric model is appropriate for a given set of data.<ref>Box-Steffensmeier, Janet M.; Jones, Bradford S. (2004) ''Event History Modeling: A Guide for Social Scientists''. Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-54673-7}} (pp. 41-43)</ref> Another example is the [[half-normal distribution]].

==Characteristics==
The generalized gamma distribution has two [[shape parameter]]s,  <math>d > 0</math> and <math>p > 0</math>, and a [[scale parameter]], <math>a > 0</math>. For non-negative ''x'' from a generalized gamma distribution, the [[probability density function]] is<ref>Stacy, E.W. (1962). "A Generalization of the Gamma Distribution." ''Annals of Mathematical Statistics'' 33(3): 1187-1192. {{JSTOR|2237889}}</ref>
:<math>
f(x; a, d, p) = \frac{(p /a^d) x^{d-1} e^{-(x/a)^p}}{\Gamma(d/p)},
</math>
where <math>\Gamma(\cdot)</math> denotes the [[gamma function]].

The [[cumulative distribution function]] is

:<math>
F(x; a, d, p) = \frac{\gamma(d/p, (x/a)^p)}{\Gamma(d/p)} , \text{or} \, 
P\left( \frac{d}{p}, \left( \frac{x}{a} \right)^p \right) ;
</math>
where <math>\gamma(\cdot)</math> denotes the [[incomplete gamma function#Lower_incomplete_gamma_function|lower incomplete gamma function]], 
and <math>P(\cdot, \cdot)</math> denotes the [[Incomplete_gamma_function#Regularized_gamma_functions_and_Poisson_random_variables|regularized lower incomplete gamma function]].

The [[quantile function]] can be found by noting that <math>F(x; a, d, p) = G((x/a)^p)</math> where <math>G</math> is the cumulative distribution function of the gamma distribution with parameters <math>\alpha = d/p</math> and <math>\beta = 1</math>. The quantile function is then given by inverting <math>F</math> using known relations about [[inverse function|inverse of composite functions]], yielding:

:<math>
F^{-1}(q; a, d, p) = a \cdot \big[ G^{-1}(q) \big]^{1/p},</math>
with <math>G^{-1}(q)</math> being the quantile function for a gamma distribution with <math>\alpha = d/p,\, \beta = 1</math>.

==Related distributions ==

* If <math>d=p</math> then the generalized gamma distribution becomes the [[Weibull distribution]].  
* If <math>p=1</math> the generalised gamma becomes the [[gamma distribution]]. 
* If <math>p=d=1</math> then it becomes the [[exponential distribution]]. 
* If <math>p=d=2</math> then it becomes the [[Rayleigh distribution]]. 
* If <math>p=2</math> and <math>d=2m</math> then it becomes the [[Nakagami distribution]]. 
* If <math>p=2</math> and <math>d=1</math> then it becomes a [[half-normal distribution]]. 

Alternative parameterisations of this distribution are sometimes used; for example with the substitution ''&alpha; &nbsp;= &nbsp; d/p''.<ref name=JK>Johnson, N.L.; Kotz, S; Balakrishnan, N. (1994) ''Continuous Univariate Distributions, Volume 1'', 2nd Edition. Wiley.  {{ISBN|0-471-58495-9}} (Section 17.8.7)</ref> In addition, a shift parameter can be added, so the domain of ''x'' starts at some value other than zero.<ref name=JK/> If the restrictions on the signs of ''a'', ''d'' and ''p'' are also lifted (but &alpha; = ''d''/''p'' remains positive), this gives a distribution called the '''Amoroso distribution''', after the Italian mathematician and economist [[Luigi Amoroso]] who described it in 1925.<ref>Gavin E. Crooks (2010), [https://threeplusone.com/pubs/on_amoroso.pdf The Amoroso Distribution], Technical Note, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.</ref>

==Moments==
If ''X'' has a generalized gamma distribution as above, then<ref name=JK/>
:<math>\operatorname{E}(X^r)= a^r \frac{\Gamma (\frac{d+r}{p})}{\Gamma( \frac{d}{p})} . </math>

==Properties==
Denote ''GG(a,d,p)'' as the generalized gamma distribution of parameters ''a'', ''d'', ''p''.
Then, given <math>c</math> and <math>\alpha</math> two positive real numbers, if <math>f \sim GG(a,d,p)</math>, then
<math>c f\sim GG(c a,d,p)</math> and
<math>f^\alpha\sim GG\left(a^\alpha,\frac{d}{\alpha},\frac{p}{\alpha}\right)</math>.

==Kullback–Leibler divergence==
If <math>f_1</math> and <math>f_2</math> are the probability density functions of two generalized gamma distributions, then their [[Kullback–Leibler divergence]] is given by
:<math>
\begin{align}
D_{KL} (f_1 \parallel f_2) 
& = \int_{0}^{\infty} f_1(x; a_1, d_1, p_1) \, \ln \frac{f_1(x; a_1, d_1, p_1)}{f_2(x; a_2, d_2, p_2)} \, dx\\
& = \ln \frac{p_1 \, a_2^{d_2} \, \Gamma\left(d_2 / p_2\right)}{p_2 \, a_1^{d_1} \, \Gamma\left(d_1 /p_1\right)} 
    + \left[ \frac{\psi\left( d_1 / p_1 \right)}{p_1} + \ln a_1 \right]  (d_1 - d_2) 
    + \frac{\Gamma\bigl((d_1+p_2) / p_1 \bigr)}{\Gamma\left(d_1 / p_1\right)} \left( \frac{a_1}{a_2} \right)^{p_2} 
    - \frac{d_1}{p_1}
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>\psi(\cdot)</math> is the [[digamma function]].<ref>C. Bauckhage (2014), Computing the Kullback–Leibler Divergence between two Generalized Gamma Distributions, {{arXiv|1401.6853}}.</ref>

==Software implementation==
In the [[R (programming language)|R]] programming language, there are a few packages that include functions for fitting and generating generalized gamma distributions. The [https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/gamlss/index.html gamlss] package in R allows for fitting and generating many different distribution families including [https://rdrr.io/cran/gamlss.dist/man/GG.html generalized gamma] (family=GG). Other options in R, implemented in the package ''flexsurv'', include the function ''dgengamma'', with parameterization: <math>\mu=\ln a + \frac{\ln d - \ln p}{p}</math>, <math>\sigma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{pd}}</math>, <math>Q=\sqrt{\frac{p}{d}}</math>, and in the package ''ggamma'' with parametrisation: <math>a = a</math>, <math>b = p</math>, <math>k = d/p</math>.

In the [[Python (programming language)|python]] programming language, [https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/tutorial/stats/continuous_gengamma.html it is implemented] in the [[SciPy]] package, with parametrisation: <math>c = p</math>, <math>a = d/p</math>, and scale of 1.
